context: The main goal we have achieved is the construction of a partial computable random sequence X which is not a.e. computably random: from the perspective of algorithmic randomness, this amounts to say that any sufficiently random sequence Z derandomizes X, in the sense that X is not computably random relative to Z. But how much randomness is actually needed to derandomize such a sequence? In particular, is Martin-Löf randomness enough? In this regard, we ask the following question. ▶ Question 1. Given a partial computably random sequence X which is not a.e. computably random, can there be a Martin-Löf random sequence Z such that X is still computably random relative to Z? If so, is there always such a Z? The second open question is more general, and strongly related with one of the main theoretical motivations leading to this work, namely the failure of the analogue of van Lambalgen’s theorem for computable randomness. Theorem 8, in fact, can be regarded as a strong failure of this result for computable randomness, because of the existence of computably random sequences that, nevertheless, can be derandomized by almost every oracle. It is known that the analogue of van Lambalgen’s theorem fails for other randomness notions studied in the literature, such as Schnorr randomness, Kurtz randomness and Demuth randomness (see [7]). However, we do not know if it fails in the strong sense mentioned above.
